topic.name: Integrating Functions by Completing the Square

question.explanation:
First, we complete the square for the expression inside the square root: \begin{align} x^2 - 8x + 15 & = x^2 - 2 \cdot 4x +(4^2 - 4^2)+ 15 \\[3pt] & = (x^2 - 8x + 16) - 16 + 15\\[3pt] & = (x-4)^2 - 1. \end{align}

Substituting the above in the given integral, we get \[ \int\dfrac{1}{|x-4|\sqrt{x^2 - 8x + 15}} \, \textrm{d}x = \int \dfrac{1}{|x-4|\sqrt {(x-4)^2 - 1} }\, \textrm{d}x. \]

This resembles the basic integral for inverse secant: \[ \int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{u^2-1}} \, \textrm{d}u = \textrm{arcsec} \, u +C \]

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $x-4.$

So, let's perform the substitution \[ u=x-4. \]

Differentiating, we get \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm{d}x = \textrm{d}u. \]

Finally, we write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate: \begin{align} \int \dfrac{1}{|x-4|\sqrt{x^2 - 8x + 15}} \, \textrm{d}x & = \int \dfrac{1}{|x-4|\sqrt{(x-4)^2 - 1} }\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \int \dfrac{1}{|u|\sqrt{u^2 - 1}} \, \textrm{d}u\\[5pt] & = \textrm{arcsec}{\,u} + C \\[5pt] & = \textrm{arcsec}(x-4) + C. \end{align}

example.title: Computing an Arcsecant Integral by Completing the Square

question.explanation:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator: \begin{align*} -x^2-4x-3& = -\left(x^2+4x +3\right) \\[5pt] & = -\left(x^2 +2 \cdot 2x +\left[2^2 - 2^2\right] +3\right) \\[5pt] %& = -[(x^2 +12x +36)-36 +35\right) \\[5pt] & = - \left((x+2)^2 -1\right) \\[5pt] & = 1 - (x+2)^2 \end{align*}

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get \[ \int_{-5/2}^{-3/2} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{-x^2-4x-3}}\, \textrm{d}x = \int_{-5/2}^{-3/2} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt {1 - (x+2)^2} } \, \textrm{d}x. \]

This resembles the basic integral for inverse sine: \[ \int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^2}}\,\textrm{d}u = \arcsin u+C \]

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $x+2.$

So, let's perform the substitution \[ u =x +2. \]

Differentiating, we get \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm{d}x = \textrm{d}u. \]

Let's use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

$x$ $-5/2$ $-3/2$
$u$ $-1/2$ $1/2$

Therefore, \begin{align*} \int_{-5/2}^{-3/2} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{-x^2-4x-3}}\, \textrm{d}x &=\int_{-5/2}^{-3/2} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x+2)^2}}\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=\int_{-1/2}^{1/2} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^2}}\, \textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &= \arcsin u \, \bigg|_{-1/2}^{1/2}\\[5pt] &=\arcsin{\left(\dfrac12\right)}-\arcsin{\left(-\dfrac12\right)} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\pi}{6} + \dfrac{\pi}{6} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\pi}{3}. \end{align*}

example.title: Computing an Arcsine Integral by Completing the Square

question.text: Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
First, we complete the square for the expression inside the square root: \begin{align} x^2+6x+8 &= x^2+2\cdot3x+(3^2-3^2)+8 \\[5pt] &= (x^2+2\cdot3x+3^2)-9+8 \\[5pt] &= (x+3)^2-1 \end{align}

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get \[ \int_{\sqrt{2}-3}^{-1} \dfrac{6}{|x+3|\sqrt{x^2+6x+8}}\,\textrm{d}x = 6\int_{\sqrt{2}-3}^{-1} \dfrac{1}{|x+3|\sqrt{(x+3)^2-1}}\,\textrm{d}x. \]

This resembles the basic integral for inverse secant: \[ \int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{u^2-1}}\,\textrm{d}u = \textrm{arcsec}\,u + C \]

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $(x+3).$

So, let's perform the substitution \[ u=x+3. \]

Differentiating, we get \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm{d}x=\textrm{d}u. \]

Let's use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

$x$ $\sqrt2-3$ $-1$
$u$ $\sqrt2$ $2$

Therefore, \begin{align} \int_{\sqrt{2}-3}^{-1} \dfrac{6}{|x+3|\sqrt{x^2+6x+8}}\,\textrm{d}x &=6\int_{\sqrt2}^{2} \dfrac{1}{|u|\sqrt{u^2-1}}\,\textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &=6\,\textrm{arcsec}\,u \,\Bigg|_{\sqrt2}^{2} \\[5pt] &=6\left(\textrm{arcsec}(2)-\textrm{arcsec}(\sqrt2)\right) \\[5pt] &=6\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) \\[5pt] &=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}. \end{align}
